<reason>Both sides executed at a high level with proper A1/A2 structure and sharp pressure questions. B's best move was the "dissolution trap" in Rebuttal 2: PRO's enforcement fallback (buy-out payments) and matching answer seem to converge on B's capacity-fund alternative. But A's closing answered that trap more cleanly than B rebutted it — a quota with a buy-out is an obligation with two modes of discharge, and the allocated share is what turns discretionary charity into a debt ("Greece asks vs. Greece is owed"). A also maintained, unneutralized, that most member states would comply and only a few would buy out, which still transforms who carries the load; B's fine-as-price analysis only addresses the refusers. B's answer to A's excellent hosting question (recognised refugees aren't the real burden; throughput is) was coherent but leaned toward defending exactly the funded concentration the motion challenges. Both had minor reference-label slips ([C1.5], [P4.1]) that roughly cancel. A's path to victory survived the exchange slightly more intact, decided by the stronger closing crystallization.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4's convergence argument — that A's teeth (fines) and matching answers collapse into B's money-and-capacity alternative — was the single most damaging move of the debate, and A5's "obligation with two ways of discharging / the payment is owed because of the quota" was the decisive counter that preserved PRO's route to victory.</best_rebuttal>
